title: Best Travel Locks 2026: 5 TSA-Approved Options Compared
description: Compare the best TSA-approved travel locks of 2026. ABUS, Master Lock, Pacsafe, and more — ranked by security, ease of use, and value for travelers.
lede: A travel lock isn't going to stop a determined thief — nothing portable will. What it does is make your bag a harder target than the unlocked bag next to it, and satisfy airline requirements for locking checked luggage. TSA agents in the US can open TSA-approved locks with a master key; non-TSA locks get cut. These five represent the full range from 'cheap but adequate' to 'meaningfully more secure' at prices that won't break your travel budget.

sections.heading: How to Choose a Travel Lock
paragraphs: The right lock depends on whether you're securing checked luggage, a hostel locker, or a day bag in transit. Each use case calls for different features — shackle length, combination vs. key, and security rating all matter differently depending on where the lock lives.

subsections.heading: TSA Approval: What It Means
paragraphs: TSA-approved locks (marked with a red diamond or Travel Sentry logo) allow airport security agents to inspect your checked luggage using a master key without destroying your lock. If you check bags in the US, Canada, or Japan, use a TSA-approved lock. For international destinations without TSA screening, any lock works — and arguably a non-TSA lock is more secure since no master key exists.

subsections.heading: Combination vs. Key Lock
paragraphs: Combination locks eliminate the risk of losing a key and are far more common for travel. Choose a combination lock with at least 3-4 dials for adequate security. Key locks offer slightly better security and faster operation but add the risk of losing the key in a foreign country — a bad day.

subsections.heading: Where You'll Use It
paragraphs: For hostel lockers, you need a longer shackle (at least 40mm) to fit through the locker hasp. For luggage zippers, a smaller padlock is neater and sufficient. For backpack security in transit, a short shackle through two zipper pulls deters casual theft. Match shackle length to your actual use case.

subsections.heading: Security Rating vs. Convenience
paragraphs: Travel locks are rated by resistance to cutting and picking — but at the price and size of travel locks, all of them can be defeated with bolt cutters in seconds. The real security value is deterrence and delay: making your bag the least convenient target. Don't put irreplaceable valuables in checked luggage regardless of the lock.

sections.heading: Bottom line
paragraphs: For most travelers, the ABUS 146TSA/40 at $12 provides all the security a travel lock realistically offers at a price where losing it doesn't sting. The Pacsafe Prosafe 750 is worth the extra cost only if you specifically need cable security for locker or backpack strap applications.

faqs.q: Do I need a TSA-approved lock?
faqs.a: If you check bags on flights within the US, Canada, or other countries that use TSA-compatible screening, yes. TSA agents can open approved locks with a master key; non-approved locks get cut open. For international travel without TSA screening, non-TSA locks offer slightly better security since no universal master key exists.

Travel locks provide deterrence, not real security. Any travel-sized padlock can be defeated with bolt cutters or basic picking tools in under a minute. Their value is making your bag a less convenient target than an unlocked bag nearby. Never keep irreplaceable items in checked luggage regardless of the lock.

faqs.q: What is the best travel lock for hostel lockers?
faqs.a: You need a lock with a shackle long enough to fit through the locker hasp — at least 38-40mm. The Pacsafe Prosafe 750 cable lock or any ABUS TSA lock with a 40mm+ shackle works well. Avoid mini locks with very short shackles that may not fit hostel lockers.

faqs.q: Can airport security open my luggage if I use a TSA lock?
faqs.a: Yes — that is the entire point of TSA approval. TSA agents have master keys that open all Travel Sentry and Safe Skies approved locks. They can inspect and re-lock your bag without cutting or breaking your lock. If you use a non-TSA lock, they will cut it and leave it open or destroyed.

faqs.q: Should I use a lock on my carry-on bag?
faqs.a: TSA prohibits locked carry-on bags that would prevent inspection during screening in the US. However, you can use a lock on your carry-on at your destination — for hostel lockers, leaving your bag in hotel storage, or locking it in your room. Just remove or unlock it before returning through airport security.

products.review: ABUS's 146TSA/40 strikes the ideal balance of build quality, ease of use, and price for a travel lock. The German engineering shows in the crisp combination reset mechanism and solid zinc body — it's meaningfully better made than cheap alternatives without approaching the price of premium options. At $12, buy two.
pros: Solid zinc alloy body — noticeably better than plastic competitors
40mm shackle fits most luggage and hostel locks
cons: No indicator when TSA has opened your bag
Single-dial wordlock alternatives may be easier to remember

products.review: Master Lock's 4693D at $10 is the utilitarian choice — widely available worldwide (so replaceable if lost), TSA-approved, and from a brand with decades of lock manufacturing behind it. The plastic body is less premium than the ABUS but works perfectly for the job. It's the travel lock you buy in bulk.
pros: Global brand — replaceable at most hardware stores
cons: Plastic body feels less durable than ABUS zinc

products.review: Pacsafe's Prosafe 750 is a TSA-approved cable lock rather than a standard padlock — the 75cm braided steel cable lets you loop through multiple zipper pulls, secure a bag to fixed furniture, or lock through hostel locker hasps that a standard padlock won't reach. The combination is easy to use one-handed.
pros: Can loop through multiple zipper pulls simultaneously
More versatile than a standard padlock
cons: Cable can be cut faster than a hardened shackle
$25 is the most expensive option here

products.review: Wordlock uses letters instead of numbers, letting you set a memorable word as your combination instead of a random 4-digit string. It's genuinely clever for travelers who routinely forget their combination mid-trip. At $9 it's the cheapest option here and works fine as a deterrent lock.
pros: Word-based combination is easier to remember than numbers
cons: Letter dials mean fewer actual combinations than they appear (dictionary words only)

products.review: Retrospec's TSA combination lock at $15 offers a directional combination wheel instead of numbered dials — you set a sequence of up, down, left, right movements that is harder to shoulder-surf than a visible number combination. A nice security feature for travelers concerned about observation in crowded airports.
pros: Directional combination is harder to observe than number dials
Compact and colorful — easy to spot your bags
cons: Directional combination takes getting used to
Less widely known brand than ABUS or Master Lock

methodology: Locks were evaluated on build quality, TSA approval status, ease of combination reset and use, shackle length for practical applications, and value at their respective price points. We did not test these products ourselves.
pinDescription: The best TSA-approved travel locks of 2026 compared — find the right lock for your luggage, hostel locker, or backpack without overpaying.
